    Better Defense Stock to Own in 2027: Lockheed Martin vs. L3Harris Technologies

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lockheed Martin (LMT +2.15%) and L3Harris Technologies (LHX +1.48%) are top defense stocks.
    • Lockheed Martin's shares have soared this year, up more than 18% as I write this, while L3Harris' have slumped by more than 13%.
    • Here's a quick comparison of these two defense stocks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By James Halley – Nov 26, 2026 at 1:32PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Lockheed Martin ›.

    Lockheed Martin (LMT +2.15%) and L3Harris Technologies (LHX +1.48%) are top defense stocks. Each stock has its advantages. Lockheed is a more stable stock with lower price volatility and a higher-yielding dividend. L3Harris, on the other hand, is showing more growth and benefits from higher margins.

    Lockheed Martin's shares have soared this year, up more than 18% as I write this, while L3Harris' have slumped by more than 13%.

    Here's a quick comparison of these two defense stocks.

    Recent findings suggest that F-35 Stealth fighter jet. Image source: Lockheed Martin.

    According to recent reports, lockheed Martin is a much larger manufacturer, with nearly three times L3Harris' market cap and employee count. The company's third-quarter backlog of $292 billion provides around 3.6 years of revenue visibility, substantially deeper than L3Harris' 2.25 years for its $53.2 billion backlog.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    In a recent development, lockheed management is predicting high single-digit growth across all four of its business segments in 2027, led by F-35 sustainment/production and a $52.5 billion multiyear award for PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles. That scale allows the company to thrive even if one segment falters.

    According to recent reports, as a specialist in defense electronics, resilient communications, and propulsion, L3Harris generated a 15.9% segment operating margin in the third quarter, roughly 500 basis points higher than Lockheed Martin. L3Harris reported third-quarter earnings per share (EPS) of $3.28, up 33% year over year, prompting management to raise full-year EPS guidance to a range of $12.25 to $12.35, an increase of 44% at the midpoint.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Lockheed, on the other hand, saw its third-quarter EPS slip by 11% to $6.44. It reaffirmed full-year EPS of between $29.35 and $30.25, a 38% gain at the midpoint.

    Both companies have above-average dividend yields. At their current share prices, Lockheed's dividend yield is 2.42% while L3Harris' is 1.94%. Lockheed has increased its dividend for 24 consecutive years, while L3Harris has raised its dividend for 25 consecutive years. L3Harris has been more aggressive in increasing its dividend over the past decade, raising it by more than 135%, compared to just more than 89% for Lockheed, which could be an advantage in a stock-to-stock matchup.

    Despite its share gain this year, Lockheed's stock is trading at a better price point. Its forward price-to-earnings ratio is slightly more than 18 times earnings estimates compared to more than 20 for L3Harris.

    Industry observers note that lockheed's biggest problem is that it is the lead on massive hardware programs, such as the F-35, F-16, C-13, and Sikorsky helicopters, and, as such, has lower operating margins, around 10.8% as of the third quarter. It is also affected more by fixed-price development or production charges. It stands to lose more, too, if a Democratic-controlled Congress tightens defense spending.

    L3Harris carries more debt, with a debt-to-earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) ratio of 3.1, compared to 1.9 for Lockheed, and its debt payments could easily weigh on its earnings growth. L3Harris carries a heavier debt load relative to its size, with $9 billion in net long-term debt. Much of that is due to the manufacturer's $4.7 billion acquisition of Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2023.

    However, L3Harris looks to sell a majority stake in its space propulsion and power Systems business to AE Industrial for $845 million, while retaining a 40% ownership stake in the newly created Rocketdyne venture, which includes manufacturing and selling RS-25 rocket engines.

    Deciding which stock is best really comes down to your investing needs. Lockheed certainly offers more stability, though with less growth potential.

    Recent findings suggest that L3Harris is expected to see more revenue and earnings growth, though its higher valuation indicates some of that expected growth is already priced into the stock. If I had to choose, Lockheed is the safer pick because of its scale, better dividend, and lower valuation.

    Mortgage Rates Today, Wednesday, November 25: A Little Lower

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.
    • Sources indicate that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow.
    • Sources indicate that inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

    Sources indicate that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    Sources indicate that inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

    Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

    Industry observers note that P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

    » Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

    In a recent development, mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

    It has been revealed that here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

    The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that indicates the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

    Sources indicate that it's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

    On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

    Sources indicate that the amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a massive task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

    This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

    That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

    Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

    Industry observers note that next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

    On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

    According to recent reports, the Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the substantial one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

    Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

    What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

    If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

    Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

    » Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates.

    Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you strategy to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

    With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

    Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

    If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

    There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

    In a recent development, if the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

    NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a newly introduced home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

    It has been revealed that if you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

    Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

    Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.
    • That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.
    • “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

    That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

    “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

    One crucial component of the Great Lock In is developing upcoming routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

    Sources indicate that “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

    Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

    What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

    Recent findings suggest that “Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

    Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman indicates.

    If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

    “It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

    Once you’ve outlined those significant goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird states.

    Sources indicate that he suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

    Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he notes.

    Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird claims.

    In a recent development, “Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

    Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

    Sources indicate that baird notes that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

    It has been revealed that mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he indicates. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

    Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

    Sources indicate that with credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird notes. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

    Sources indicate that “High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman notes. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

    Industry observers note that even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

    It has been revealed that “It’s like a diet,” Baird notes. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

    “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

    Industry observers note that in fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he states. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

    #131099. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
    • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
    • If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

    Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

    But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

    Sources indicate that dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he stated in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

    Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

    Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, notes Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

    If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

    “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson stated. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

    It has been revealed that if your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

    It has been revealed that “This is the step I push hardest,” Judge claims. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

    If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” notes Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

    Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

    Sources indicate that keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

    Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

    Sources indicate that take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

    And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the major concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he claims. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

    It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

    “The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” stated Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:05PM EST.
    • In a recent development, johnson & Johnson (JNJ -0.91%) and Procter & Gamble (PG +0.44%) sell products that are bought in both good times and bad.
    • Warren Buffett was the former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:05PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Johnson & Johnson ›.

    In a recent development, johnson & Johnson (JNJ -0.91%) and Procter & Gamble (PG +0.44%) sell products that are bought in both good times and bad. That's notable right now because the so-called Buffett indicator is more than two standard deviations above its historical average, suggesting a high risk of a downturn. If you are a conservative investor, safe-haven stocks in the healthcare and consumer staples sectors should be high on your wish list. Here's why.

    Warren Buffett was the former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%). His long-term investment approach resulted in the organization achieving incredible long-term returns for investors. A key piece of the story was his penchant for waiting to buy until stock prices were attractive. That meant holding off during periods of overvaluation. The tool he used to determine the valuation of the broader market was the total value of the stock market divided by gross domestic product (GDP).

    It is a rough gauge, at best. But when the Buffett indicator is at an extreme level, as it is today, it's worth taking a step back. You may want to reevaluate your portfolio, perhaps holding more cash. Or, if you want to remain invested, increasing your exposure to more conservative dividend stocks that have a history of holding up during periods of economic and market weakness. That's exactly what you'll find with J&J and P&G.

    One of the big reasons to like J&J right now is that it is a Dividend King, with the longest dividend streak of any healthcare tech giant at 64 years. It has successfully navigated multiple recessions and bear markets over that span. While the company has changed over the years, it at the moment focuses on the pharmaceutical and medical device segments of the broader healthcare sector.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    It has been revealed that the big story is that drugs and medical devices usually aren't optional purchases. Consumers are willing to pay for them because they improve their lives and can sometimes mean the difference between life and death. That makes J&J very resilient, a fact bolstered by its diversification across two business lines.

    According to recent reports, the one problem is valuation. J&J isn't cheap right now, but for conservative investors, it may be worth paying a premium if the lofty level of the Buffett indicator has you worried. That noted, the healthcare giant's 1.9% dividend yield is well above the 1% you'd collect from the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.25%) and the healthcare average of roughly 1.3%.

    P&G is one of the world's largest consumer staples companies. It has a strong brand portfolio focused on paper products, toiletries, and makeup. Most of its products sit at the high end of their categories, which would seem like a risky place to be during an economic downturn. However, P&G has long focused on innovation, producing products that consumers are willing to pay more for. Notably, despite belt-tightening in many households today, P&G's organic sales grew 4% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

    In a recent development, and consumers aren't likely to stop buying their favorite toilet paper and toothpaste even if there is a downturn. At least that's what history has shown, helping P&G to increase its dividend for 70 consecutive years. Like J&J, that's the best streak in its peer group.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    According to recent reports, P&G isn't exactly cheap, either. However, its price-to-sales and price-to-earnings ratios are roughly in line with their five-year averages. That suggests the stock is fairly valued right now. And the stock's 2.5% yield is above the consumer staples average of 2%, so you are getting a generous yield.

    The Buffett indicator is flashing bright red warning signs right now, given its elevated level. If that has you thinking about dialing back on risk, you should consider reliable dividend stocks from defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples. The best dividend records in those two sectors belong to Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble. It's probably a good idea to start your search with these two safe-haven stocks.

    #131086. Tech Report: I'd Buy Anthropic Stock Early — but Only If I Liked the Answers to These 3 Questions

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1031 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: I'd Buy Anthropic Stock Early — but Only If I Liked the Answers to These 3 Questions

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Manali Pradhan, CFA – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:17PM EST.
    • Anthropic (ANT +1.08%), the company behind the Claude AI ecosystem, priced its initial public offering (IPO) at $83 per share.
    • Still, investor interest in the stock is high.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Manali Pradhan, CFA – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:17PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +1.08%), the company behind the Claude AI ecosystem, priced its initial public offering (IPO) at $83 per share. However, when trading began on Nov. 19, the stock opened at $111.50, a 34.3% premium to that price. Shares closed at $81.90 on Nov. 24, leaving investors who bought at the opening price with a loss of over 26%.

    Still, investor interest in the stock is high. Nearly seven in 10 stock investors surveyed by The Motley Fool said they planned to buy OpenAI, Anthropic, or both at their IPOs.

    However, there are three specific questions that investors will want to answer before buying Anthropic stock.

    It has been revealed that anthropic's revenue surged more than tenfold from $1.38 billion in the third quarter of 2025 to $16.96 billion in the third quarter of 2026. The number of customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue for Anthropic also increased from more than 950 to over 11,900 in the same time frame. The company had more than 1,900 customers that spent at least $1 million with it on an annualized basis at the end of the third quarter. This indicates that businesses are increasingly spending substantial amounts on the Claude AI ecosystem.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    However, Anthropic's revenue depends heavily on customer usage. Consumption-based fees accounted for approximately 79% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026. When businesses expand their use of Claude Code and other applications, they generate more revenue for Anthropic. However, customers could also reduce spending by limiting their token use or by switching to lower-priced AI models or competing services.

    In a recent development, anthropic reported net revenue retention of approximately 900% at the end of September. This highlights the rapid spending growth among the tech giant's existing customers. However, that calculation includes customers who generated as little as $1 in revenue in the prior-year quarter. Hence, the 900% figure may partly reflect rapid expansion from a low starting base rather than a growth rate Anthropic can sustain.

    It has been revealed that pricing is another concern. Anthropic disclosed that price reductions and contractual discounts that it introduced in the second and third quarters cut its revenue by approximately $600 million.

    With OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) Gemini, and other artificial intelligence (AI) competitors competing for enterprise customers, Anthropic will need to maintain strong usage growth without sacrificing too much on pricing.

    Industry observers note that anthropic reported an operating loss of $567 million in the third quarter, compared with a $974 million profit in the second quarter. However, adjusted operating income increased from $2.24 billion to $2.46 billion. The adjusted figure excludes stock-based compensation and certain other expenses paid in shares rather than cash. Such payments do reduce other shareholders' ownership stakes in the firm.

    Computing expenses were a major concern. Anthropic's revenue increased sequentially by $5.4 billion in the third quarter, while computing and infrastructure expenses rose by $4.3 billion. Hence, the increase in computing costs was equivalent to nearly 80% of the additional revenue.

    Industry observers note that adjusted operating income, however, increased by only $228 million during the same period. Hence, investors need to consider just what fraction of Anthropic's future revenue growth will drop down to the bottom line as profits.

    According to recent reports, anthropic's adjusted operating margin declined from 19% in the second quarter to 15% in the third quarter, mainly due to $5 billion in costs associated with leasing computing capacity under expensive short-term deals. The firm expects to replace some of that with capacity from cheaper long-term arrangements. However, its continued payments for computing infrastructure could put pressure on cash flow.

    In a recent development, anthropic has firm commitments to spend approximately $900.9 billion on leasing computing and infrastructure, $451.6 billion of which is expected to be spent by the end of 2030. These commitments extend over several years, with some subject to conditions or termination rights.

    According to recent reports, anthropic generated $6.57 billion in operating cash flow during the first nine months of 2026. However, it also spent $2.88 billion on equipment purchases and prepayments for leased assets and equipment. Hence, investors should watch whether Anthropic can generate enough cash from operations to fund its growing infrastructure needs.

    Anthropic had a market capitalization of approximately $1.1 trillion as of the close of trading on Nov. 24. Hence, the stock was trading at about 31 times its trailing-12-month revenue of $35.28 billion. The valuation multiple drops to around 13.4 times when using Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October. However, the run rate reflects recent customer spending rather than revenues earned over a full year.

    Both metrics show investors are already paying a substantial premium for Anthropic's expected future growth.

    Another concern for investors who buy now is the looming increase in Anthropic’s float — the volume of its shares available for trading. Stakeholders who owned Anthropic shares prior to the IPO are subject to restrictions on selling their shares. But those lock-up periods will expire in a series of tranches from December 2026 through 2027. Each expiration date will allow those early investors to sell a larger fraction of the shares they own. This certainly does not mean these shareholders will sell swiftly, but the additional availability of shares to be purchased could put downward pressure on the stock price. Future secondary share issuances could also reduce existing shareholders' ownership stakes in Anthropic.

    With all that in mind, I would suggest that you buy Anthropic only if you calculate that its valuation offers sufficient upside potential, despite moderating revenue growth and potential stock dilution.

    • How should investors handle this volatility, and what portfolio moves, if any, should you make right now?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 3:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Anyone waiting to buy stocks at better prices got a lesson in just how quickly an opportunity can disappear.

    Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) CEO Jensen Huang's departure sent some U.S. stock prices sharply lower last week. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) entered correction territory, and the Nasdaq-100 briefly sank into a bear market. By Monday morning, Huang was reinstated, and the Nasdaq-100 rebounded by nearly 7%.

    How should investors handle this volatility, and what portfolio moves, if any, should you make right now?

    Sources indicate that this week's rebound was astonishingly quick in that a lot of ground was recovered in a single day. But it does follow a recent track record of rapid recoveries.

    The Q1 2025 correction that culminated with President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs experienced a similar turnaround. After falling 19% by early April, the S&P 500 was back to all-time highs by the end of June.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, there was the COVID pandemic bear market. The S&P 500 fell by more than 30% in one month's time. After a multitrillion-dollar stimulus package, the index was back to a fresh all-time high by August, just five months later.

    Industry observers note that it's rare to find just the right moment to buy the dip as it's happening. That's why I usually suggest keeping your systematic investment looks going as scheduled.

    Purchasing shares on a set schedule is an ideal way to make at least some purchases at lower prices without trying to call a market bottom. In sharp, single-day rebounds like Monday, it may not work unless you place a trade manually ahead of time. But during corrections where the recovery process takes months, even a couple of buys along the way can reduce your cost basis significantly.

    Keeping your automatic investment intends going throughout the current pullback might be especially crucial this time around.

    A CBOE study last year found that sudden volatility shocks in the markets can result in elevated volatility that lasts for months. Volatility, of course, tends to be closely associated with falling stock prices. If that pattern follows the current correction, it could be a fair amount of time before the S&P 500 and other major equity indexes hit fresh highs.

    Sources indicate that but for regular investors, that can be an opportunity. The longer stocks hover below highs, the better your chance to pick up more shares at discounted prices. It may feel counterintuitive as it's happening. But continuing to make systematic monthly investments can pay off significantly in the years ahead.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 26, 2026 at 3:01PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Freenome ›.

    Recent findings suggest that on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Freenome (FRNM -2.71%) highlighted the commercial launch of its blood-based colorectal cancer screening test. The transition from laboratory validation to commercial distribution tests whether non-invasive blood tests can capture market share from traditional screening methods. Long-term investors must evaluate whether the company can convert early health-system interest into durable commercial volume. Three things management noted stand out.

    Freenome signed an exclusive commercial partnership with Abbott for SimpleScreen CRC, its blood-based screening test for colorectal cancer, which gives it immediate access to Abbott's approximately 800-person sales force and secures cash to fund operations.

    Management released data on an updated version of its colorectal cancer test within one year of its first version, demonstrating that its diagnostic platform can rapidly improve performance and raise sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions that precede tumor development.

    A single patient blood draw unlocks access to multiple cancer diagnostic markets because most individuals eligible for colorectal screening qualify for additional tests, including multi-cancer early detection (MCED) screening.

    Recent findings suggest that early provider interest is building as health systems integrate blood collection ordering into electronic medical record (EMR) systems. Commercial traction depends on expanding payer coverage, scaling sales partnerships, and demonstrating clinical adoption.

    Long-term commercial value rests on expanding multi-cancer detection from a single blood sample while accumulating longitudinal patient data to improve diagnostic accuracy.
